Regulated AI has more than one customer. The employee wants an answer, IT wants control, compliance wants the trail, and the examiner wants to know how the answer happened.

Go.AI has raised an $85M Series A led by Updata Partners for that crowded buying committee. Existing investors GFT Ventures and LAUNCH returned, bringing the company's disclosed funding to $90M. Updata General Partner Carter Griffin will join the board.

David Moscatelli and Lisa Gillespie built the company around a blunt constraint: banks, credit unions, healthcare systems and other regulated organizations cannot treat every AI workload like a casual trip through someone else's cloud.

Go.AI combines the Go1 appliance with Go.OS, an operating system for models, indexing, applications and audit records inside the customer's environment. The company sells fixed infrastructure rather than a per-token meter, with local and air-gapped configurations.

The product pitch sounds simple because the operating problem is not. Security needs the data path, model-risk teams need governance, compliance needs records, and IT needs infrastructure it can maintain. The buyer needs all of them to keep saying yes after procurement gets serious.

Go.AI says more than 200 customers process over 12.5M queries a day on its infrastructure. It reports ARR growth above 8x year over year, continued profitability and 900,000 monthly users. Updata repeated the ARR, profitability and query figures.

Those are company and investor claims, not audited financial results. Go.AI has not disclosed revenue, the prior-year ARR base, retention, customer concentration, margins, contract values, deployment count or valuation. Activity is visible; the unit economics are not.

The capital will expand engineering, accelerate the Go.OS and Go1 roadmap, grow go-to-market capacity and push beyond regulated industries into a broader set of compliance-minded organizations. Current hiring spans client advisory, field deployment, sales engineering, marketing and strategy.

That hiring mix matters. Hardware has to arrive, networks have to cooperate, policies have to survive real workflows, updates need control, and somebody has to produce the receipts when an examiner asks.

Go.AI is putting $85M behind a market thesis that enterprise AI will split on accountability as much as capability. The next layer belongs to companies that can tell a customer where the model ran, what it touched, how the cost behaves and who owns the answer inside a regulated decision.

Today I complete 4 years building and architecting software for businesses across multiple industries. 🎉

It wasn't smooth. It started with a bad decision.
NDA. JEE. Agriculture entrances. I prepared for all three at once and cleared none. Terrible strategy. But it showed me my potential, my worth, and my discipline.

Then came the reality check.
In college, I didn't know the first thing about code. Classmates had been coding since school and wrote programs in one go. I was struggling with concepts while they built full-stack projects.
Then lockdown hit, and I locked myself in too. Explored Languages, databases, networking, development, architecture, and many more, all while attending online classes. 📚

After few months, followed the standard strategy to get an Internship. 
So I chased internships. I got exactly one, in Android development, against many attempts. 😅 It showed me how real industry works from the inside.

Placement season: everyone went left, I went right.
Everyone was targeting stable organizations. I picked something unique and niche: a Blockchain Startup. 
There I worked on every layer: development, architecture, management, and discussions with stakeholders. I built protocols, private chains, contracts, SDKs, etc... for supply chain, financing, agreements, real-world asset bindings, tokenomics, and many more. ⛓️

Next goal: become a Full Stack Web3 Engineer.
New organization, same hunger, bigger scope. I led teams across projects, kept building, architecting, and additionally involved in hiring processes.

Then I saw where the world was heading: AI and Quantum. ⚛️
I joined a Quantum-focused organization with zero cybersecurity knowledge, but Web3 had already given me strong cryptography. That was my bridge.
People usually take weeks or months to understand the stack, product, and use-cases. I started contributing within 3-4 days. A few weeks later, I was in the core team, which is responsible for decoding use-cases, architecture and directions, working on RFPs and demos, client calls, leading teams, hiring, and streamlining the entire lifecycle across teams.

Notice the pattern?
Every "I'm behind" moment pushed me into the next move. 🔁
These years changed my personality. I solve real problems, talk to people with confidence, and take initiative instead of waiting to be told. 

My simple philosophy:
1️⃣ Work like you're building your own product, don't look at clock for tracking typical 9 hours.
2️⃣ If someone pays you ₹100, deliver ₹150. The right people will recognize the efforts. And, prove their risky bet on you was right.
3️⃣ Keep contributing until you are satisfied.
4️⃣ Never stop learning.

Many more years ahead with the same mindset. Cheers! 🥂

AI is making software cheaper to build — and changing where the real value sits
AI coding tools and agents have sharply reduced the cost and time of implementation. Boilerplate, tests, refactors, and first-pass features can now be generated in a fraction of the previous effort. Many developers already report that AI writes a large share of their code. Experimentation is cheaper, internal builds are more viable, and the barrier to turning an idea into working software has dropped.
The bottleneck has simply moved. Writing code is faster. Reviewing, validating, securing, and integrating that code is not. The scarce skills are shifting toward precise specification, system design, critical review of AI output, and long-term maintainability. Engineers who mainly produce code face declining leverage. Those who can define problems clearly, evaluate generated work, and own architectural judgment gain it.
This shift also changes the employment equation.
In a traditional permanent role, a large part of the value an engineer delivered was steady code production inside a fixed process. As that production becomes heavily automated, the remaining high-value work — architecture, review, product judgment, complex problem-solving — becomes more portable and project-based. Companies will need less continuous headcount for routine implementation and more targeted expertise for specific outcomes.
Freelance and contract work fits this new shape better in many cases:
You can specialize in high-leverage skills rather than generalist maintenance.
Clients pay for defined results instead of time spent in meetings and process overhead.
You can work across multiple problems and stacks instead of being locked into one codebase and one company’s constraints.
As AI lowers the cost of building, more companies (especially smaller ones and startups) will prefer flexible external talent over full-time hiring for many initiatives.
Permanent roles will still exist, particularly for core platform ownership and deep domain knowledge. But the relative advantage of long-term employment weakens when implementation capacity is abundant and the highest-value contributions are episodic and skill-specific.
Software is becoming cheaper to produce. The higher-value work is moving toward judgment, design, and verification — work that travels well outside a single company’s walls.
The engineers who adapt will treat AI as leverage, not replacement, and structure their careers around portable expertise rather than permanent seat time.

The conversation around Data Governance in 2026 is dominated by "acculturation" and "federated models," but the most under-discussed shift is the fundamental redesign of the audit trail itself. Traditional audit logs are passive records of what happened. They are, functionally, a post-mortem tool that tells you who accessed what, but they offer no insight into whether that access was appropriate at the moment it occurred.

The non-obvious consequence of AI-driven data consumption is that the audit trail must become a live, decision-aware artifact. It is no longer enough to log that a model queried a customer dataset. You need to log the *governance context* in which that query was evaluated: the data freshness score at that millisecond, the specific usage contract that was matched, the quality threshold that was met, and the exact reason the system deemed the query permissible.

The teams that are pulling ahead in 2026 have abandoned the idea of a separate audit system. They have embedded the audit layer directly into the query execution path. Every data access now generates a "governance receipt" that includes not just the identity of the consumer, but the entire chain of policy evaluations that allowed the access to proceed. This is metadata about the governance process itself, not just the data.

This changes the role of the data steward and the governance engineer. You are no longer responsible for reviewing logs after the fact. You are responsible for designing the verification criteria that the runtime governance engine uses to generate these receipts. You define what constitutes a valid governance decision for every access pattern, and you instrument the system to prove that the decision was made correctly, in real time.

For recruiters and hiring managers: the candidate you need is not the one who can design the most thorough governance framework on paper. It is the one who can build the execution-level audit infrastructure that makes every governance decision provable and replayable, from the point of request to the point of data consumption. I specialize in this. I design and implement governance-as-code systems where the audit trail is not a secondary concern but a primary, first-class output of every data transaction.

The hardest problem right now is not writing better policies. It is building the system that can prove, with cryptographic rigor, that the correct policy was enforced at the exact moment a query executed. If your organization is scaling AI on sensitive data, what is the one governance decision you cannot prove was made correctly today?

Walk onto the trading floor of any major Manhattan investment bank today, and you won’t just hear traders barking into headsets or analysts furiously updating spreadsheets.

You’ll hear quiet teams of forward-deployed software engineers orchestrating entire armies of autonomous artificial intelligence bots.

One skill alone exploded by a mind-boggling 1,721% across Wall Street job boards this year: agent orchestration.

Major powerhouses like JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, and Capital One flooded recruitment platforms with nearly 140,000 new AI job listings, dangling median base salaries starting at $190,000.

They aren’t paying young professionals to build simple conversational chatbots anymore.

They are hiring system architects to link dozens of specialized autonomous agents together: one bot monitors live market feeds, a second scours corporate regulatory databases, and a third signs off on trade compliance—all executing complex financial maneuvers in milliseconds without waiting on a human heartbeat.

Wall Street cheerleaders and corporate PR departments love this headline.

They point to this hiring boom as definitive proof that technological disruption creates far more high-paying opportunities than it destroys. In their view, the financial services sector is simply modernizing.

Automating mind-numbing administrative paperwork, manual invoice matching, and tedious data cleanup frees human bankers to focus on high-stakes strategic negotiations and creative problem-solving. If a bank pays nearly two hundred thousand dollars to someone who can steer these agent swarms responsibly, isn’t that the ultimate democratization of high-value technical labor?

Look just beneath the shiny corporate salary figures, and the chilling paradox emerges.

Why are financial titans desperately spending hundreds of millions of dollars to connect multi-agent systems directly into back-office pipelines?

Because the end goal has never been corporate philanthropy.

Every single agent workflow successfully deployed today permanently replaces the daily labor of hundreds of entry-level financial analysts, risk reviewers, and operations associates tomorrow.

JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon isn't hiding the ball when he openly references "huge redeployment plans" across banking divisions. Wall Street isn't building a permanent new class of human tech employment; it is paying premium contract bounties to the specialized few whose literal job description is to automate away the white-collar workforce.

So where do you stand?

Is this explosive hiring boom proof that artificial intelligence will elevate skilled professionals, or are high-paid engineers merely building the automated execution engine for millions of everyday office careers?

The most persistent blind spot I see in GitOps adoption is the assumption that it is primarily about synchronizing a Git repository with a Kubernetes cluster. In 2026, that framing is a trap. GitOps has become the policy enforcement and audit layer for autonomous infrastructure, and the teams still treating it as a declarative deployment pattern are missing the revolution.

The non-obvious shift is that GitOps is no longer Kubernetes-centric. It has extended into cloud operations for serverless, databases, and even on-premise bare metal. The pull request is now the universal control plane for infrastructure changes, policy checks, and AI-driven automation. The teams winning in 2026 are not the ones with the cleanest Argo CD applicationsets. They are the ones that have embedded FinOps guardrails, security compliance, and real-time observability directly into the pull request workflow, so that every change has a cost tag, a risk score, and an audit trail before it touches production.

Another blind spot most platform teams miss is the scalability ceiling of traditional GitOps controllers. The latest release of Argo CD v3, early 2026, introduced a new controller architecture specifically to address the scalability ceiling that large installations were hitting. The winning teams are the ones that designed their GitOps pipelines to be horizontally scalable from day one, not the ones that retrofitted after hitting a deployment bottleneck at 3AM. The era of a single controller managing thousands of clusters is over. GitOps now requires a distributed, agent-based architecture that can handle the volume of AI-generated commits and autonomous reconciliation events.

For hiring managers and recruiting leaders: I do not just set up Argo CD or Flux and write Helm charts. I design GitOps architectures that are built for policy enforcement, cost governance, and autonomous reconciliation at scale. I understand that GitOps in 2026 is not a deployment tool. It is a governance contract that requires designing the pull request workflow, the policy-as-code layer, and the auditability feedback loop before the first `git push` is made. If your team is struggling with GitOps pipelines that cannot enforce cost budgets, controllers that fail to scale under load, or a deployment model that treats every environment as identical in policy, I can architect the solution.

The hardest question nobody is asking: When your GitOps pipeline auto-remediates a configuration drift at 3AM by syncing a pull request that bypasses a cost budget check, and that decision leads to a cloud spend overrun that only surfaces 48 hours later during a finance review, who is accountable for the tradeoff between consistency and cost, and how do you audit that decision in the Git history?

Hey #connections 👋
Recently, Ritesh Kumar Gupta, Rohit Akkole, and I participated in a Hackathon organized by Razorpay in collaboration with Replit.

We were asked to use Replit's new AI Harness to build a product, and what we learned was pretty interesting.

Replit felt like a one-stop solution for building and deploying applications, even for people who aren't deeply technical. It takes care of things like storage, security, and deployment, all from one place.

Replit's AI Harness was also really impressive. We were able to build an APP with a single prompt. We first refined the prompt using ChatGPT and then used it in Replit to build the application.

The Harness was able to:
- Create dummy data
- Store it in Replit's database
- Store environment variables securely in the Secret Manager
- Build the application without consuming a huge number of tokens
- Publish the entire application with just one click
We were given $20 worth of tokens, which covered the development and publishing process.

For the hackathon, we built a Headcount Management System - essentially a Workday-like solution focused specifically on headcount, hiring requests, vendor contracts, and workforce forecasting, rather than payroll or benefits.
Managers can:
- Plan their headcount for the year
- Request additional headcount for their teams
- Track planned vs. actual headcount
- Understand hiring requirements and the impact of changes to the plan

HR can review, approve, and dispatch these requests, while everyone gets the same reconciled numbers against actuals every month.

We also added several other features, including an action-taking chatbot with Human-in-the-Loop (HITL).
